In [[ring theory]], a subfield of [[abstract algebra]], a '''right Kasch ring''' is a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] ''R'' for which every [[simple module|simple]] right ''R''-[[module (mathematics)|module]] is [[isomorphic]] to a right [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] of ''R''.<ref>This ideal is necessarily a [[minimal right ideal]].</ref> Analogously the notion of a '''left Kasch ring''' is defined, and the two properties are independent of each other.

Kasch rings are named in honor of mathematician [[Friedrich Kasch]]. Kasch originally called [[Artinian ring]]s whose proper ideals have nonzero [[annihilator (ring theory)|annihilator]]s ''S-rings''.<ref>{{harv|Kasch|1954}}</ref><ref>{{harv|Morita|1966}}</ref> The characterizations below show that Kasch rings generalize S-rings.

==Definition==
Equivalent definitions will be introduced only for the right-hand version, with the understanding that the left-hand analogues are also true. The Kasch conditions have a few equivalent statements using the concept of [[annihilator (ring theory)|annihilator]]s, and this article uses the same notation appearing in the annihilator article.

In addition to the definition given in the introduction, the following properties are equivalent definitions for a ring ''R'' to be right Kasch. They appear in {{harvtxt|Lam|1999|loc=p. 281}}:
# For every simple right ''R''-module ''M'', there is a nonzero [[module homomorphism]] from ''M'' into ''R''.
# The [[maximal ideal|maximal]] right ideals of ''R'' are right annihilators of ring elements, that is, each one is of the form <math>\mathrm{r.ann}(x)</math> where ''x'' is in ''R''.
# For any maximal right ideal ''T'' of ''R'', <math>\mathrm{\ell.ann}(T) \neq \{0\}</math>.
# For any proper right ideal ''T'' of ''R'', <math>\mathrm{\ell.ann}(T) \neq \{0\}</math>.
# For any maximal right ideal ''T'' of ''R'', <math>\mathrm{r.ann}(\mathrm{\ell.ann}(T)) = T</math>.
# ''R'' has no [[dense submodule|dense]] right ideals except ''R'' itself.

==Examples==
The content below can be found in references such as {{harvtxt|Faith|1999|loc=p. 109}}, {{harvtxt|Lam|1999|loc=§§8C,19B}}, {{harvtxt|Nicholson|Yousif|2003|loc=p.51}}.

*Let ''R'' be a [[semiprimary ring]] with [[Jacobson radical]] ''J''. If ''R'' is [[commutative ring|commutative]], or if ''R''/''J'' is a [[simple ring]], then ''R'' is right (and left) Kasch. In particular, commutative [[Artinian ring]]s are right and left Kasch.
* For a [[division ring]] ''k'', consider a certain [[subring]] ''R'' of the 4-by-4 [[matrix ring]] with entries from ''k''. The subring ''R'' consists of matrices of the following form:
:: <math>\begin{bmatrix}
a & 0 & b & c \\
0 & a & 0 & d \\
0 & 0 & a & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & e \end{bmatrix}</math>
:This is a right and left Artinian ring which is right Kasch, but ''not'' left Kasch.
* Let ''S'' be the ring of [[power series]] on two noncommuting variables ''X'' and ''Y'' with coefficients from a [[field (mathematics)|field]] ''F''. Let the ideal ''A'' be the ideal generated by the two elements ''YX'' and ''Y''<sup>&thinsp;2</sup>. The [[quotient ring]] ''S''/''A'' is a [[local ring]] which is right Kasch but ''not'' left Kasch.
* Suppose ''R'' is a [[direct product of rings|direct product]] of infinitely many nonzero rings labeled ''A''<sub>k</sub>. The [[direct sum]] of the ''A''<sub>k</sub> forms a proper ideal of ''R''. It is easily checked that the left and right annihilators of this ideal are zero, and so ''R'' is not right or left Kasch.
* The 2-by-2 upper (or lower) [[triangular matrix]] ring is not right or left Kasch.
* A ring with right [[Socle (mathematics)#Socle of a module|socle]] zero (i.e. <math>\mathrm{soc}(R_R)=\{0\}</math>) cannot be right Kasch, since the ring contains no [[minimal ideal|minimal]] right ideals. So, for example, [[domain (ring theory)|domain]]s which are not division rings are not right or left Kasch.
